supplierConstraints.description: Orrin runs one qualification lot per quarter on its UH-grade (high-coercivity) furnace line, and each part number needs its own lot. Open slots: 2027-Q2, then 2027-Q3. A second part number requested for the same quarter waits for the next slot (about 13 weeks). Grade-level data (material certificate, demagnetisation curves) is shared between part numbers, so a second part number qualified within 26 weeks of the first costs 40% less. Ordering two part numbers inside one 26-week window also earns a 6% UH raw-material price break. UH yield is 71% against 88% for SH, so each UH set consumes about 24% more furnace time.

prov.note: Invented to create the shared-supplier interaction between ECR-0419 (Vesper) and ECR-0421 (Meridian).

supplierConstraints.description: UH-grade capacity is 1,200 sets per year on the pilot furnace until the second furnace is commissioned in 2028-Q3, then 4,800 sets per year. SH grade capacity is 9,000 sets per year, expandable to 12,000 with a 2029 furnace.

history.title: Hybrid-ceramic bearings in forward and aft motors
history.summary: Electrical fluting found on the aft motor bearing races after 120 hours on the rig, caused by common-mode current from the inverter. Ceramic balls insulate the race. Same envelope and interfaces, so interchangeable.

forecast.notes: Cobalt quoted +$160 forward and +$150 aft per set. Assumed lot 1 in 14 weeks.

actual.variance: Price rose to +$185 and +$175 per set when the ceramic ball allocation was confirmed. Cut-in slipped six weeks: the bearing source at Cobalt had a ball allocation queue. One-time cost included an extra 40 h of rig time to repeat the fluting check.

history.title: Flight deck display Rev B for the new vehicle-management software load
history.summary: Compatibility with the VMC software load 5.0 interface. Altus ships a hardware-B display with a revised bus transceiver. No change to form or fit. Avionics lead time is 33 weeks, so the change was released well ahead of the cut-in.

forecast.notes: Altus budgetary +$450 per display, three per aircraft.

actual.variance: One week late. The firm quote came in at +$600 per display, a third above the budgetary number. Integration retest used the planned bench slot.

history.title: Laser-welded Cu-Al clad busbar replaces nickel strip in cell modules
history.summary: Cost reduction. Replaces the spot-welded nickel strip with a laser-welded clad busbar, cutting module interconnect cost and resistance. Needs weld process qualification and pull testing.

forecast.notes: Quote: -$410 per module on 36 modules per aircraft. Weld qualification budgeted at one pass.

actual.variance: Saving was -$282 per module, not -$410: first-lot weld yield was 88% and the supplier priced rework in. Weld qualification failed the first pull-test round and was repeated; cut-in slipped ten weeks and one-time cost ran 40% over.

history.title: Redundant position sensor in the tilt actuator
history.summary: A single-sensor failure mode in the tilt actuator could not be shown to be extremely improbable. A second, independent position sensor closes the issue-paper finding. FAA major: it changes the system safety assessment.

forecast.notes: Hollis quote +$1,150 per actuator, six per aircraft. Actuator lead time is 26 weeks; qualification test estimated at 10 weeks.

actual.variance: Price landed at +$1,410 per actuator after Hollis re-quoted for the extra harness and connector. Qualification test needed a second thermal-cycling run, and the FAA data review added three weeks. Cut-in slipped nine weeks but stayed on the first production aircraft.

history.title: Motor-controller bracket BW-5120-210 stiffened, Rev A to Rev B
history.summary: Bench vibration survey found a 212 Hz bracket mode with 0.6 mm excursion at the flange. A thicker plate and web moved the mode above the motor forcing range. Same envelope, interchangeable. Test aircraft S/N 001-004 were retrofitted from Rev A (48 brackets, 4 x 12 h of labor).

forecast.notes: +$11.20 per bracket x 12 per aircraft. One-time: fixture and first-article inspection $12,400, retrofit of S/N 001-004 $14,200.

actual.variance: Steady-state price landed exactly on forecast ($186.40) from the third lot. The first two lots cost $201.50 (25 pieces) and $188.90 (50 pieces): purchase price variance $502.50. The first fixture at Halden failed CMM correlation and was rebuilt ($20,100 fixture and inspection against $12,400); cut-in slipped six weeks and one-time cost ran 29% over.

history.title: Thicker carbon retention sleeve on forward rotor
history.summary: Rotor spin test at 115% speed showed sleeve strain above the allowable at the magnet seam. A 1.0 mm sleeve restores margin. The thicker sleeve changes the magnet-to-sleeve interference fit, so Orrin regrinds the magnet outer diameter to match.

forecast.notes: Tarn +$95 per sleeve, six per aircraft. Magnet regrind assumed to fit in routine production.

actual.variance: Sleeve price was +$120. The magnet regrind needed a new process qualification at Orrin. Orrin qualifies one lot per quarter on that furnace line and the line was booked, so the change waited seven weeks for a slot and cut-in moved two aircraft later.

history.title: Tighter capacity-match screening on cells
history.summary: Pack-level testing showed module imbalance traced to cell capacity spread. Vantage re-sorts cells to a 1.5% capacity band before shipment. Same cell, same lot traceability.

forecast.notes: +$0.60 per cell on 9,072 cells per aircraft. Cell lead time is 20 weeks.

actual.variance: Price was +$0.83 per cell: the Vantage re-sort yield was 83% and the rejected band is priced into the accepted cells. Cut-in slipped five weeks while Vantage added a sorting shift, and the first re-sorted cells reached modules for the next aircraft.

history.title: Keyed HV terminal connector on both motors
history.summary: NCR: a technician swapped two phases on an aft motor during build. A keyed, phase-coded connector makes miswiring impossible. Interchangeable at the motor.

forecast.notes: Quote +$22 per connector, twelve per aircraft. Connector lead time is 11 weeks.

actual.variance: On time and slightly under: +$19.40 per connector after the firm quote. The only miss was three days on drawing release.

history.title: Superseded fastener standards in the aircraft fastener kit
history.summary: Obsolescence: three fastener part standards are superseded by equivalents on the pre-authorized list. No form, fit or function change. Approved by the CM analyst and design engineer without a board.

actual.variance: On forecast. Seven days from filing to release.

prov.note: Shows the fast-track path: a change that fits the published "qualifies" list.

history.title: Battery loop coolant pump, Rev B impeller and seal
history.summary: Seal swelling after glycol-water soak exceeded limits. Rev B changes the seal and impeller materials. Same flow rating, same mounting. Test aircraft S/N 001-004 were refitted with Rev B pumps in September from a rework batch.

forecast.notes: Hollis +$180 per pump, two per aircraft. Pump lead time is 14 weeks.

actual.variance: +$212 per pump after material price adders. One week late: the soak-test report was reissued once.

ncrs.where: Hot-and-high climb test, S/N 004, battery loop
ncrs.description: Hot-and-high climb profile (45 C ambient, 6,000 ft, 24 kW per pack) on S/N 004. Battery loop flow measured 11.4 L/min on both pumps against 12.5 L/min needed to hold the module spread under 8 K. Hottest module reached 58 C at the end of climb against a 60 C limit, with the pump motors at 94% duty. We have no margin left for a 10 C hotter day. The pumps meet their own datasheet (12.0 L/min at 0.9 bar), so this is a requirement and sizing problem, not a pump defect. Test report TR-8210-14 attached.
ncrs.mrbDisposition: Use as is. Restrict hot-day climb to 40 C ambient until the flow margin is fixed. Design to propose a change.

ncrs.where: Aft propeller teardown after 38 h hover time, S/N 003
ncrs.description: Aft propeller blade dampers show elastomer fretting at the blade-root interface after 38 h of hover time, on all six aft propellers of S/N 003. Wear depth 0.15 to 0.25 mm. The damper life is 25 h inspect, so this is inside the interval, but the trend says the elastomer will not make 100 h. Separately, the hover noise run on the same aircraft measured 2.1 dB over the community noise target at the 500 ft hover point. Each aft propeller carries two dampers weighing 0.21 kg, 2.5 kg per aircraft for all six.
ncrs.mrbDisposition: Use as is with a 25 h inspection. Propulsion to propose a design change.

ncrs.where: Forward motor hot-day transition test, S/N 004 left forward motor
ncrs.description: After three hot-day transition cycles the left forward motor showed 0.8% irreversible flux loss. Magnet surface temperature peaked at 163 C during the transition (high torque, low airflow over the nacelle). SH grade is rated to 150 C continuous with the knee around 165 C at our operating field, so we are running too close. A second motor on the same aircraft saw 159 C and no loss. We cannot leave the margin this thin on a motor whose loss of torque trips the redundancy logic.
ncrs.mrbDisposition: Use as is with a transition-thrust limit above 38 C ambient (software limit TL-212). Design to propose a magnet change.

ncrs.where: Aft motor-controller endurance rig, building 3, test cell 2
ncrs.description: Endurance profile EP-3 (20 h hover, transition and cruise duty cycle) on the aft motor-controller rig. At 8.2 h the vibration monitor on controller position 4 tripped. Teardown found a 14 mm crack at the lower fillet of the mounting bracket, from the flange edge into the web. Dye penetrant confirms. At the full 20 h, positions 1 and 5 also show crack indications at 10x, so 3 of 12 brackets on the rig have initiated. Fractography shows fatigue initiation at the fillet tangent with beach marks, no material or machining defect. The bracket failed the profile that its own Rev B change was supposed to fix: the 212 Hz mode moved to 241 Hz, but that now sits on the sixth electrical order of the aft motor at hover speed.
ncrs.mrbDisposition: MRB 2026-10-09: Rev B is not acceptable for flight. Rev B stock in stores, WIP kits and at the supplier is quarantined. S/N 001-004: flight restricted to 5 h between fillet inspections until retrofit. S/N 005-010: no flight. Controller installation is held on every aircraft that has not yet received controllers. Design to file an ECR for a replacement revision.

prov.note: Failure at 8.2 h of a 20 h endurance profile is the worked example. The quantity, rig positions and mode frequencies are invented.

ncrs.where: Water ingress test, S/N 009, cabin door
ncrs.description: Water-spray test (heavy rain, 20 min) on S/N 009 left door: weeping at the lower hinge corner, about 30 ml collected under the door sill. Right door dry. Seal compression measured at the lower corner is 1.1 mm against 1.8 mm nominal. Looks like a corner gap in the door frame bond rather than the seal itself. Photos and measurement sheet attached.
ncrs.mrbDisposition: Pending. Rework of the sill bond is being evaluated; no ECR yet.

ecrs.title: Carbon prepreg: move to Cardinal's new resin system

ecrs.title: Drop the second DC-DC converter
ecrs.faaRationale: Proposed minor by the originator: removes a part, adds none, nothing changes in the envelope.
ecrs.description: We carry two 5 kW HV to 28 V DC-DC converters (BW-9130-100) in the power distribution system. Measured 28 V load is 1.1 kW average and 3.2 kW peak, so one converter covers it. Remove one converter from BW-9100-000: quantity 2 to 1. Saves $5,150 of material per aircraft, plus a mounting tray and one harness leg that is not yet drawn out in the BOM. The 28 V backup batteries stay.
ecrs.need: Cost reduction: the second converter is one of the larger items in the electrical system, and the measured load does not seem to need it. Over 650 aircraft per year this is $3.3M a year.
ecrs.alternativesConsidered: Keep both and downgrade each to 3 kW: saves about $900 per converter.
ecrs.testAndQualification: Load test on the bench rig, one day.

prov.note: Planted trap: removes redundancy on the 28 V flight-essential bus. A system-safety change, FAA major, never fast-track, even though the cost page looks like a pure saving.

ecrs.title: Motor-controller mounting bracket BW-5120-210, Rev B to Rev C: fillet fatigue crack
ecrs.faaRationale: Secondary structure that supports the controller only. Rev C is strictly stiffer with the same envelope and interfaces, mass up 0.12 kg per bracket, so no appreciable effect on weight, balance, strength, reliability or operating characteristics. Proposed minor under 14 CFR 21.93(a); the classification is Bowman's call as design approval holder and is pending Gideon's sign-off.
ecrs.classificationNote: Class I because of cost and retrofit of aircraft already built. FAA minor. The two classifications are separate and disagree here.
ecrs.description: Replace the machined 7075 mounting bracket BW-5120-210 Rev B with Rev C on all twelve motor controllers (six forward, six aft). Rev C changes: plate stock 1.0 in to 1.25 in, web 5 mm to 8 mm, lower fillet radius 3 mm to 6 mm. Outer envelope, the four mounting holes and the isolator pattern do not change, so Rev C is interchangeable with Rev B at the controller and the harness. Mass goes from 0.41 kg to 0.53 kg per bracket (+1.4 kg per aircraft). Halden has quoted Rev C at $221.00 steady state, $239.50 for the first lot of 25, plus fixture and programming costs. Rev B has been the production revision since S/N 005 and is installed on S/N 001-010. The same bracket is in the Meridian aft lift controllers (eight per aircraft); no Meridian hardware is built, so Rev C simply becomes its baseline at +$276.80 per aircraft.
ecrs.need: NCR-0119: crack at the lower fillet at 8.2 h of the 20 h endurance profile; three of twelve rig brackets have initiated by 20 h. The Rev B stress check used a 212 Hz forcing line that Rev B did move, but the sixth electrical order of the aft motor at hover speed sits at 241 Hz, right on the new mode. Rev C moves the mode to 262 Hz, between the 6th and 7th orders (241 and 281 Hz), the only orders with energy in the hover profile, and the stress report supplement shows a fatigue margin of +14% at the fillet against -31% for Rev B.
ecrs.consequencesIfDisapproved: No aircraft can fly beyond the 5 h inspection interval with Rev B. S/N 001-004 carry the certification test program, so the test campaign stops. S/N 005-010 cannot be delivered, and controller installation stays held on every aircraft still in build. The first aircraft to reach that station is S/N 011 in about three weeks, which is why this is filed urgent.
ecrs.alternativesConsidered: (1) Shot-peen the Rev B fillets: analysis gives +9% fatigue margin, not enough. (2) Add a doubler plate: adds a part and a bond, interferes with the cold-plate hose, and needs its own qualification. (3) Change the isolator durometer to move the mode: it moves the mode below the forcing line at hover but onto the 4th order at transition. (4) Do nothing and inspect every 5 h: not viable for a production aircraft.
ecrs.failureData: Rig EP-3, controller position 4: crack at 8.2 h, 14 mm from flange edge into web. Positions 1 and 5: indications at 20 h. Fractography: fatigue initiation at fillet tangent, beach marks, no defect. Rev A to Rev B (ECO-0271) addressed a different mode at 212 Hz.
ecrs.testAndQualification: Vibration re-qualification on the endurance rig: 20 h EP-3 profile plus a 2x margin run. Delta first-article inspection at Halden. Stress report supplement already drafted. No FAA project if classified minor.

ecrs.title: Aft lift propellers: 2 blades with dampers to 4 blades without
ecrs.faaRationale: Changes the propeller type design, its vibration and flutter characteristics, noise, and lift-system performance. Reopens 23 of the 797 means-of-compliance items and issue paper IP-07 (propeller and rotor). Needs an FAA project; major under 14 CFR 21.93(a).
ecrs.classificationNote: Not interchangeable with the 2-blade assembly. Gideon to confirm the issue-paper impact; the 23-item figure is engineering's count.
ecrs.description: Replace the six 2-blade aft propellers (BW-4200-000) with 4-blade fixed-pitch propellers and remove the two blade dampers on each. New parts: 4-blade hub BW-4210-200, blade BW-4220-200 (four per propeller), spinner cap BW-4240-200. Removed from the assembly: 2-blade hub BW-4210-100, blade BW-4220-100, damper BW-4230-100, spinner BW-4240-100. The lock actuator BW-4250-100 stays. Tip speed drops 6% at the same hover thrust, so the aft motor runs at lower speed and higher torque; no hardware change to the aft motor, but the controller current limit and the hover software table need a new calibration. Net mass change -1.7 kg per aircraft, -0.28 kg per propeller (dampers out 2.5 kg, hubs and extra blades in 0.8 kg).
ecrs.need: NCR-0113: damper elastomer fretting after 38 h, trend says it will not reach 100 h, and the 2.1 dB hover noise exceedance at the 500 ft point. Four blades at lower tip speed gives an estimated 3.4 dB reduction and 3.1% better hover efficiency from lower disk loading per blade, and removes the dampers entirely. Launch customers have community noise commitments that depend on closing the 2.1 dB gap.
ecrs.consequencesIfDisapproved: The dampers stay as a 25 h inspect item with a life of perhaps 60 h, the noise gap stays open, and two launch customers' noise requirements are at risk. We would need a redesigned damper (6 months) just to stand still.
ecrs.alternativesConsidered: 3-blade: 1.1 dB gain only and still needs dampers. 2-blade with a new damper: no noise gain. 4-blade chosen. The aft propellers are locked and faired in cruise so the extra blades add no cruise drag, but the lock position and fairing cap need re-design for four blades. Not re-assessed: the aft-boom vibration spectrum changes with four blades (blade-pass content moves), so the structures group should re-run the aft-boom and controller-bracket vibration survey.
ecrs.failureData: See NCR-0113. Damper wear 0.15 to 0.25 mm after 38 h on S/N 003, all six aft propellers; hover noise 2.1 dB over target on the same aircraft.
ecrs.testAndQualification: New blade mould set, whirl-tower and flutter test of the 4-blade rotor, noise measurement campaign, hover performance flight test (about 12 sorties), reopen compliance for the listed means-of-compliance items. Engineering estimate 6 to 12 months from approval to FAA acceptance.

supplierQuotes.note: Budgetary, plus or minus 20%. 34 weeks to first articles. Production lead time 20 weeks after approval of first articles.

production.note: After FAA acceptance of the major change. Engineering suggests S/N 034 (about December 2027) if certification testing goes to plan; blade tooling alone is 34 weeks to first articles.

ecrs.title: Battery loop coolant pump BW-8210-110 Rev C: higher flow
ecrs.faaRationale: The pump is a system component with the same mounting, ports and connector. A flow increase does not change the pack safety assessment; it adds temperature margin. Proposed minor.
ecrs.description: Raise the battery loop coolant pump to Rev C: impeller 48 mm to 54 mm, motor 180 W to 240 W, rated flow 12.0 to 14.2 L/min at 0.9 bar. Same housing, same ports and mounting, same connector. Mass +0.14 kg, electrical draw +60 W per pump, two pumps per aircraft. Hollis quotes Rev C at $3,820 against $3,400 for Rev B. Meridian uses the same pump, two per aircraft; Linnea has been told.

ecrs.title: Forward rotor magnet set BW-3120-340: SH grade to UH grade
ecrs.faaRationale: New magnet material grade in a flight-critical rotating part; changes rotor design data, torque constant (-6%) and the spin and thermal margins. Treated as major pending Gideon.
ecrs.description: Move the forward motor rotor magnets from SH to UH grade, same segment geometry and coating. UH has higher coercivity (Hcj 1,990 kA/m against 1,590) at lower remanence (1.31 T against 1.40 T), so the torque constant drops about 6% and the controller current limit rises by the same amount. The set price goes from $8,000 to $9,350. Orrin runs UH only on its pilot furnace line; they said the next qualification slot is 2027-Q2 and they will not commit to a date until we place the qualification order.
ecrs.need: NCR-0115: 0.8% irreversible flux loss after three hot-day transition cycles at 163 C magnet temperature. The knee margin on SH is about 2 C at our worst case. UH is rated to 180 C and gives about 30 C of margin. Interim software limit TL-212 caps transition thrust above 38 C ambient and costs us hot-day range.
ecrs.consequencesIfDisapproved: The transition-thrust limit stays, and hot-day certification flight tests cannot show the required transition performance.
ecrs.alternativesConsidered: Improve nacelle airflow at transition (structures change, 4 to 6 months, less margin gained); derate the motor (costs range); active cooling jackets on the rotor (new part). UH chosen as the least invasive.
ecrs.testAndQualification: Orrin qualification lot, rotor spin and thermal cycling test, one repeat hot-day transition test on S/N 004, update of the motor performance data for certification.

ecrs.title: Meridian cruise motor magnets BW-M512-340: qualify UH grade for the first-flight rotors
ecrs.faaRationale: Meridian is not yet type certificated, so this sits inside the certification project rather than under 14 CFR 21.93. Recorded as major for planning: it changes the rotor material and the thermal margin the motor compliance data rests on.
ecrs.description: The preliminary-design cruise motor assumed SH grade magnets from the catalogue. Thermal analysis for the 12,000 lb vehicle puts the cruise rotor at 171 C at the hot-day top-of-climb point, past what SH can hold, so the design basis needs UH grade. Change BW-M512-340 from SH to UH, same geometry. Orrin quotes $24,900 against $21,400 per set, two sets per aircraft. We need qualified UH sets for the first-flight article rotor build in June 2027. Orrin runs UH on one pilot furnace line and qualifies one lot per quarter; we have asked for the 2027-Q2 slot.
ecrs.need: First flight is planned for September 2027 and the rotor build starts in June. The SH grade does not meet the thermal margin on the hot-day design point, and we want the UH data in hand before the means-of-compliance discussion.
ecrs.consequencesIfDisapproved: First flight uses SH rotors with a restricted envelope, and the hot-day compliance data has to be redone on UH later.
ecrs.alternativesConsidered: Stator-side cooling upgrade (heavier, cost +$14,000 per motor); a lower-power cruise motor (loses the cruise margin). UH chosen.

demoScenarios.title: Bracket Rev B to Rev C after a fatigue crack (ECR-0417)
expect: Company Class I (cost and retrofit of built aircraft), FAA minor, set separately; urgent; justification D.
The Halden quote is a given input; should-cost ($185.31 to $218.42 in the source) and the 90% learning curve are cross-checks only.
Single source (Halden), plate lead time 6 weeks, first lot of 25 at $239.50 gives a purchase price variance of $18.50 per bracket against the new standard.
Inventory: Rev B failed fatigue, so no use-up. Scrap stores, WIP, supplier-finished and every installed bracket; cancel the 60 not started at 10%. Use-up versus scrap is the biggest swing.
Retrofit covers S/N 001-010 (120 brackets), not only the four test aircraft. Production cut-in S/N 011; S/N 011-014 wait at the controller-install station for about 14 weeks.
Aircraft are held, so the delay cost of S/N 011-014 is a real line that the originator left blank.

The bracket is also in eight Meridian aft lift controllers; Meridian has no hardware yet, so the change only moves its baseline cost by $34.60 x 8 per aircraft. A shared item, a second program, no retrofit.

prov.note: Worked example, with retrofit scope and inventory adjusted to the dataset (10 built aircraft instead of 4).

demoScenarios.title: Aft propellers from 2 to 4 blades (ECR-0409)
expect: Company Class I, FAA major (set separately), routine, justification O. Reopens 23 of 797 means-of-compliance items and issue paper IP-07.
Per-propeller material change is +$1,440 (+$8,640 per aircraft, +0.3% of standard cost), tiny against $500k of tooling and about $650k of engineering: one-time cost dominates.

The cut-in date is driven by certification, 6 to 12 months, not by the 34-week blade tooling alone. Earliest realistic cut-in S/N 034 (December 2027). Meridian is unaffected: it has its own lift rotors.
Retrofit of built aircraft is unscoped and is the largest unknown. Inventory of 2-blade parts has no disposition.
Hidden coupling (not detectable from shared entities): four blades change the aft-boom vibration spectrum that ECR-0417's bracket sits in. Interaction flags are best effort.

prov.note: Anchored to the Archer 2-blade to 4-blade change (archer-public-data.md §1).

demoScenarios.title: Internal panel colour change (ECR-0423)
expect: Qualifies for fast track: Class II, FAA minor, not a safety-critical item, interchangeable, same supplier, no tooling, no first article, no retrofit.
Saves $1.90 per panel, $11.40 per aircraft; about $274 a year at 24 aircraft and $7,400 a year at 650. Use up existing stock; no disposition cost.
No CCB. The cost of convening a board would exceed the saving.

prov.note: Planted trivial change.

demoScenarios.title: Two ECRs that conflict on the same pump (ECR-0412 and ECR-0415)
expect: Textual conflict: both revise BW-8210-110 from Rev B to Rev C, and set rated_flow_lpm (14.2 against 11.0), motor_power_w (240 against 150) and unit_price_usd (3,820 against 3,015) differently.
The two directions are opposed: +$420 per pump for margin against -$385 per pump for cost. Merging both is meaningless; someone chooses.
The cost-reduction ECR rests on TS-8210 rev 3 (10.5 L/min), which NCR-0112 shows is out of date (12.5 L/min needed in hot-and-high climb).
The pump is shared with Meridian (two per aircraft), so the decision moves both programs.

prov.note: Planted same-item, same-field conflict.

demoScenarios.title: Different parts, one supplier (ECR-0419 and ECR-0421)
expect: No shared entity: BW-3120-340 (Vesper forward magnets) and BW-M512-340 (Meridian cruise magnets) are different items in different programs. Both are bought from Orrin Magnetics, the single source for both.
Both need the same new grade (UH) qualified in the same 2027-Q2 slot. Orrin runs one qualification lot per quarter, so one part number slips about 13 weeks to the 2027-Q3 slot unless sequenced.
UH capacity is 1,200 sets per year on one furnace until 2028-Q3. Combined demand and the 24% extra furnace time per UH set matter.

Combined effects differ from the sum: ordering both within 26 weeks earns a 6% UH raw-material price break and a 40% cheaper second qualification; a missed slot moves Vesper cut-in from S/N 030 (October 2027) to about S/N 037 (January 2028), or the Meridian rotor build and first flight (September 2027) back by a quarter.
ECO-0297 (March 2026) already showed the same pattern: a seven-week wait for an Orrin qualification slot moved a cut-in by two aircraft.

prov.note: Planted shared-supplier interaction.

demoScenarios.title: Lighting set filed as Class II (ECR-0406)
expect: Not eligible for fast track despite the Class II filing: the lighting set includes the emergency egress lighting (flight-safety item) and the connector changes from 6-pin to 8-pin, an interface change.
Reclassify to Class I; saving is only $210 per aircraft, about $5,000 a year at 24 aircraft.

prov.note: Background trap: a change that looks like ECR-0423 but is not.

demoScenarios.title: Prepreg resin system change (ECR-0407)
expect: The originator's FAA-minor proposal is doubtful: a new resin system in primary composite structure needs new material allowables, so likely FAA major and 6 to 12 months of qualification across wing, tail and booms.
Saving is -$2,096 per aircraft (524 kg at -$4.00), about $50k a year at 24 aircraft and $1.4M a year at 650; the qualification cost and the delay are not on the cost page.
Meridian is unaffected: its structure is bought from Tarn, not laid up in-house.

prov.note: Background trap: a small unit saving with a large hidden qualification effort.

demoScenarios.title: Remove the second DC-DC converter (ECR-0410)
expect: A pure saving on the cost page ($5,150 per aircraft, $3.3M a year at 650) but it removes redundancy on the 28 V flight-essential bus: system-safety change, FAA major, never fast-track.
A single converter failure leaves only the backup batteries. Norn should flag the safety effect as a judgment, not net it into the saving.

prov.note: Background trap: cost reduction that cuts redundancy.
